claim: Coagulopathy is a significant aspect of morbidity in COVID-19 patients.
source: Coagulopathy is a significant aspect of morbidity in COVID-19 patients.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws from established clinical observations about COVID-19.

claim: The clotting cascade is propagated by a series of proteases, including factor Xa and thrombin.
source: The clotting cascade is propagated by a series of proteases, including factor Xa and thrombin.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the coagulation cascade.

claim: TMPRSS2 and furin are known to be important for cleavage activation of SARS-CoV-2 spike to promote viral entry in the respiratory tract.
source: While certain host proteases, including TMPRSS2 and furin, are known to be important for cleavage activation of SARS-CoV-2 spike to promote viral entry in the respiratory tract, other proteases may also contribute.
evidence: This statement references established knowledge from prior research.

claim: Factor Xa and thrombin can directly cleave SARS-CoV-2 spike.
source: Using biochemical and cell-based assays, we demonstrate that factor Xa and thrombin can also directly cleave SARS-CoV-2 spike, enhancing infection at the stage of viral entry.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Factor Xa and thrombin enhance SARS-CoV-2 infection at the stage of viral entry.
source: Using biochemical and cell-based assays, we demonstrate that factor Xa and thrombin can also directly cleave SARS-CoV-2 spike, enhancing infection at the stage of viral entry.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Coagulation factors increased SARS-CoV-2 infection in human lung organoids.
source: Coagulation factors increased SARS-CoV-2 infection in human lung organoids.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: A drug-repurposing screen identified a subset of protease inhibitors that promiscuously inhibited spike cleavage by both transmembrane serine proteases and coagulation factors.
source: A drug-repurposing screen identified a subset of protease inhibitors that promiscuously inhibited spike cleavage by both transmembrane serine proteases and coagulation factors.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: The mechanism of nafamostat and camostat may extend beyond inhibition of TMPRSS2 to coagulation-induced spike cleavage.
source: The mechanism of the protease inhibitors nafamostat and camostat may extend beyond inhibition of TMPRSS2 to coagulation-induced spike cleavage.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing these inhibitors affect both TMPRSS2 and coagulation factors.

claim: Anticoagulation is critical in the management of COVID-19.
source: Anticoagulation is critical in the management of COVID-19, and early intervention could provide collateral benefit by suppressing SARS-CoV-2 viral entry.
evidence: This is a statement based on clinical knowledge and the implications of the study findings.

claim: Early anticoagulation intervention could provide collateral benefit by suppressing SARS-CoV-2 viral entry.
source: Anticoagulation is critical in the management of COVID-19, and early intervention could provide collateral benefit by suppressing SARS-CoV-2 viral entry.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the study findings.

claim: Infection-induced hypercoagulation exacerbates SARS-CoV-2 infectivity through a positive feedback mechanism.
source: We propose a model of positive feedback whereby infection-induced hypercoagulation exacerbates SARS-CoV-2 infectivity.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings and represents speculation about the mechanism.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 emerged into the human population in late 2019.
source: SARS-CoV-2 emerged into the human population in late 2019 and has evolved into a devastating global health crisis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the timeline of the COVID-19 pandemic.

claim: Limited world-wide vaccine distribution is a concern for COVID-19 management.
source: Despite the recent success of vaccines (Baden et al., 2021; Polack et al., 2020), the limited world-wide vaccine distribution (Kwok et al., 2021; Lin et al., 2020; Nhamo et al., 2021; So and Woo, 2020), the emergence of viral variants (Wang et al., 2021; Weisblum et al., 2020), and the repeated SARS-like zoonotic outbreaks over the last 20 years (Cheng et al., 2007; Ge et al., 2013; Menachery et al., 2015) underscore the urgent need to develop antivirals for coronavirus (Pan et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The emergence of viral variants underscores the urgent need to develop antivirals for coronavirus.
source: Despite the recent success of vaccines (Baden et al., 2021; Polack et al., 2020), the limited world-wide vaccine distribution (Kwok et al., 2021; Lin et al., 2020; Nhamo et al., 2021; So and Woo, 2020), the emergence of viral variants (Wang et al., 2021; Weisblum et al., 2020), and the repeated SARS-like zoonotic outbreaks over the last 20 years (Cheng et al., 2007; Ge et al., 2013; Menachery et al., 2015) underscore the urgent need to develop antivirals for coronavirus (Pan et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Repeated SARS-like zoonotic outbreaks have occurred over the last 20 years.
source: Despite the recent success of vaccines (Baden et al., 2021; Polack et al., 2020), the limited world-wide vaccine distribution (Kwok et al., 2021; Lin et al., 2020; Nhamo et al., 2021; So and Woo, 2020), the emergence of viral variants (Wang et al., 2021; Weisblum et al., 2020), and the repeated SARS-like zoonotic outbreaks over the last 20 years (Cheng et al., 2007; Ge et al., 2013; Menachery et al., 2015) underscore the urgent need to develop antivirals for coronavirus (Pan et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Coronaviruses require proteolytic processing of the spike protein by host cell proteases to facilitate membrane fusion and viral entry.
source: In addition to attachment to specific receptors on target cells, coronaviruses require proteolytic processing of the spike protein by host cell proteases to facilitate membrane fusion and viral entry (Glowacka et al., 2011; Jaimes et al., 2020c; Walls et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In SARS-CoV-2, host cell proteases act on two sites: the S1/S2 subunit boundary and the S2' region proximal to the fusion peptide.
source: In SARS-CoV-2, host cell proteases act on two sites residing at the S1/S2 subunit boundary and at the S2' region proximal to the fusion peptide (Belouzard et al., 2009; Hoffmann et al., 2020a; Jaimes et al., 2020b; Millet and Whittaker, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: S1/S2 site cleavage opens up the spike trimer and exposes the S2' site.
source: S1/S2 site cleavage opens up the spike trimer and exposes the S2' site, which must be cleaved to allow for the release of the conserved fusion peptide (Benton et al., 2020; Madu et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The S2' site must be cleaved to allow for the release of the conserved fusion peptide.
source: S1/S2 site cleavage opens up the spike trimer and exposes the S2' site, which must be cleaved to allow for the release of the conserved fusion peptide (Benton et al., 2020; Madu et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The prevailing model suggests that furin cleaves the S1/S2 site and TMPRSS2 cleaves the S2' site.
source: While the prevailing model suggests that furin cleaves the S1/S2 site and TMPRSS2 cleaves the S2' site (Bestle et al., 2020), it remains unclear to what extent other proteases may be involved (Hoffmann et al., 2021; Ou et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: It remains unclear to what extent other proteases may be involved in SARS-CoV-2 spike cleavage.
source: While the prevailing model suggests that furin cleaves the S1/S2 site and TMPRSS2 cleaves the S2' site (Bestle et al., 2020), it remains unclear to what extent other proteases may be involved (Hoffmann et al., 2021; Ou et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature and represents a knowledge gap.

claim: TMPRSS2 is an important host cell factor in proteolytic activation across multiple coronaviruses.
source: TMPRSS2 is an important host cell factor in proteolytic activation across multiple coronaviruses (Hoffmann et al., 2020a; Jaimes et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: TMPRSS2 knockout or inhibition reduces infection in mouse models of SARS and MERS.
source: TMPRSS2 knockout or inhibition reduces infection in mouse models of SARS and MERS (Iwata-Yoshikawa et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: TMPRSS2 has been highlighted as a drug target for SARS-CoV-2.
source: More recently, TMPRSS2 has been highlighted as a drug target for SARS-CoV-2 (Hoffmann et al., 2020a; Hoffmann et al., 2020b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Furin activity is not essential to produce infectious particles.
source: Furin activity is not essential to produce infectious particles (Tang et al., 2021a) and furin is not necessary for cell fusion (Papa et al., 2021), but deletion of the S1/S2 site attenuates SARS-CoV-2 in vivo (Johnson et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Furin is not necessary for cell fusion.
source: Furin activity is not essential to produce infectious particles (Tang et al., 2021a) and furin is not necessary for cell fusion (Papa et al., 2021), but deletion of the S1/S2 site attenuates SARS-CoV-2 in vivo (Johnson et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Deletion of the S1/S2 site attenuates SARS-CoV-2 in vivo.
source: Furin activity is not essential to produce infectious particles (Tang et al., 2021a) and furin is not necessary for cell fusion (Papa et al., 2021), but deletion of the S1/S2 site attenuates SARS-CoV-2 in vivo (Johnson et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Furin cleavage during viral biogenesis may render SARS-CoV-2 spike less stable in solution and reduce the likelihood to reach and interact with target cells.
source: Furin cleavage during viral biogenesis, before release of viral particles, may render SARS-CoV-2 spike less stable in solution and reduce the likelihood to reach and interact with target cells (Amanat et al., 2021; Berger and Schaffitzel, 2020; Wrobel et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature and represents a hypothesis.

claim: The full spectrum of proteases that catalyze biologically relevant activity at the S1/S2 site in the lung remains incompletely defined.
source: Although the S1/S2 site is often referred to as the 'furin site' (Johnson et al., 2021), the full spectrum of proteases that catalyze biologically relevant activity in the lung remains incompletely defined.
evidence: This statement represents a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: Proteases orchestrate the coagulation pathway via a series of zymogens that are each activated by a chain reaction of proteolytic processing.
source: Proteases also orchestrate the coagulation pathway, via a series of zymogens that are each activated by a chain reaction of proteolytic processing.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the coagulation cascade.

claim: Coagulopathy and thromboembolic events have emerged as a key component of COVID-19 pathogenesis.
source: Coagulopathy and thromboembolic events have emerged as a key component of COVID-19 pathogenesis (McGonagle et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Comorbidities associated with severe COVID-19 are linked to dysregulated blood clotting.
source: Comorbidities associated with severe COVID-19 are also linked to dysregulated blood clotting (Zhou et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Patients with a history of stroke prior to infection have nearly twice the risk of in-hospital mortality.
source: Patients with a history of stroke prior to infection have nearly twice the risk of in-hospital mortality (Qin et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Elevated D-dimer levels upon hospital admission are predictive biomarkers of severe disease and lethality in COVID-19 patients.
source: Upon hospital admission, elevated D-dimer levels (an indicator of fibrinolysis and coagulopathy) and low platelet counts (an indicator of consumptive coagulopathy) are predictive biomarkers of severe disease and lethality in COVID-19 patients (Zhou et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Low platelet counts upon hospital admission are predictive biomarkers of severe disease and lethality in COVID-19 patients.
source: Upon hospital admission, elevated D-dimer levels (an indicator of fibrinolysis and coagulopathy) and low platelet counts (an indicator of consumptive coagulopathy) are predictive biomarkers of severe disease and lethality in COVID-19 patients (Zhou et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Systemic activity of clotting factors V, VIII, and X are elevated in severe COVID-19 disease.
source: Systemic activity of clotting factors V, VIII, and X are elevated in severe COVID-19 disease (Stefely et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Early phase COVID-19 disease is typically restricted to a local pulmonary hypercoagulable state.
source: While early phase disease is typically restricted to a local pulmonary hypercoagulable state, late-stage disease may be accompanied by systemic DIC, stroke, and cardio-embolism (Huang et al., 2020; Kipshidze et al., 2020; McGonagle et al., 2020; Tsivgoulis et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Late-stage COVID-19 disease may be accompanied by systemic DIC, stroke, and cardio-embolism.
source: While early phase disease is typically restricted to a local pulmonary hypercoagulable state, late-stage disease may be accompanied by systemic DIC, stroke, and cardio-embolism (Huang et al., 2020; Kipshidze et al., 2020; McGonagle et al., 2020; Tsivgoulis et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Ischemic stroke occurred in approximately 1% of hospitalized COVID-19 patients.
source: Ischemic stroke occurred in approximately 1% of hospitalized COVID-19 patients, and strikingly, a fraction of them experienced stroke even prior to onset of respiratory symptoms (Yaghi et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: A fraction of COVID-19 patients experienced stroke even prior to onset of respiratory symptoms.
source: Ischemic stroke occurred in approximately 1% of hospitalized COVID-19 patients, and strikingly, a fraction of them experienced stroke even prior to onset of respiratory symptoms (Yaghi et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Multiple direct-acting anticoagulants have anti-TMPRSS2 off-target effects.
source: In a drug-repurposing effort to target TMPRSS2, we observed that multiple direct-acting anticoagulants have anti-TMPRSS2 off-target effects.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the drug screen presented in the manuscript.

claim: Circulating proteases involved in blood clotting can cleave and activate SARS-CoV-2 spike, enhancing infection at the stage of viral entry.
source: Circulating proteases involved in blood clotting can cleave and activate SARS-CoV-2 spike, enhancing infection, specifically at the stage of viral entry.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Nafamostat may incorporate a combined mechanism in the treatment of COVID-19 through inhibition of TMPRSS2 and coagulation factors.
source: We propose that the serine protease inhibitor nafamostat may incorporate a combined mechanism in the treatment of COVID-19 through inhibition of TMPRSS2 and coagulation factors.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental findings.

claim: Camostat resulted in strong inhibition of TMPRSS2.
source: Camostat and nafamostat resulted in strong inhibition of TMPRSS2 (Figure 1B), as expected (Hoffmann et al., 2020a; Hoffmann et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and citations to prior literature.

claim: Nafamostat resulted in strong inhibition of TMPRSS2.
source: Camostat and nafamostat resulted in strong inhibition of TMPRSS2 (Figure 1B), as expected (Hoffmann et al., 2020a; Hoffmann et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and citations to prior literature.

claim: Otamixaban inhibits TMPRSS2 enzymatic activity in vitro.
source: We also identified that otamixaban and the active form of dabigatran (but not its prodrug dabigatran etexilate) inhibit TMPRSS2 enzymatic activity in vitro (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: The active form of dabigatran inhibits TMPRSS2 enzymatic activity in vitro.
source: We also identified that otamixaban and the active form of dabigatran (but not its prodrug dabigatran etexilate) inhibit TMPRSS2 enzymatic activity in vitro (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: Dabigatran etexilate does not inhibit TMPRSS2 enzymatic activity in vitro.
source: We also identified that otamixaban and the active form of dabigatran (but not its prodrug dabigatran etexilate) inhibit TMPRSS2 enzymatic activity in vitro (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: Camostat, nafamostat, otamixaban, and dabigatran etexilate suppressed SARS-CoV-2 S-pseudotyped HIV-1 pseudoviral entry in Calu3 cells.
source: Consistent with the TMPRSS2 enzymatic assay, camostat, nafamaostat, otamixaban, and dabigatran etexilate suppressed pseudoviral entry, as indicated by nanoluciferase luminescent signal (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: No effects on relative cell growth were observed at the same timepoint in Calu3 cells treated with protease inhibitors.
source: No effects on relative cell growth were observed at the same timepoint in Calu3 (Figure 1F) or A549 cells (data not shown), confirming that reduced luminescent signal was not due to cytotoxicity.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Reduced luminescent signal from protease inhibitor treatment was not due to cytotoxicity.
source: No effects on relative cell growth were observed at the same timepoint in Calu3 (Figure 1F) or A549 cells (data not shown), confirming that reduced luminescent signal was not due to cytotoxicity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cell growth data.

claim: Camostat has a submicromolar IC50 for inhibiting SARS-CoV-2 pseudovirus entry in Calu3 cells.
source: A dose-response experiment with select protease inhibitors revealed a submicromolar IC50 for camostat and nafamostat and IC50s in the 10–20 µM range for otamixaban and dabigatran in Calu3 cells (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Nafamostat has a submicromolar IC50 for inhibiting SARS-CoV-2 pseudovirus entry in Calu3 cells.
source: A dose-response experiment with select protease inhibitors revealed a submicromolar IC50 for camostat and nafamostat and IC50s in the 10–20 µM range for otamixaban and dabigatran in Calu3 cells (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Otamixaban has an IC50 in the 10-20 µM range for inhibiting SARS-CoV-2 pseudovirus entry in Calu3 cells.
source: A dose-response experiment with select protease inhibitors revealed a submicromolar IC50 for camostat and nafamostat and IC50s in the 10–20 µM range for otamixaban and dabigatran in Calu3 cells (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Dabigatran has an IC50 in the 10-20 µM range for inhibiting SARS-CoV-2 pseudovirus entry in Calu3 cells.
source: A dose-response experiment with select protease inhibitors revealed a submicromolar IC50 for camostat and nafamostat and IC50s in the 10–20 µM range for otamixaban and dabigatran in Calu3 cells (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: HIV-1NL/SARS-CoV-2 pseudovirus infection is dependent on ACE2.
source: Using A549 cells with or without ectopic ACE2 expression, we confirmed that HIV-1NL/SARS-CoV-2 pseudovirus infection is dependent on ACE2, while infection with HIV-1NL pseudotyped instead with VSV G envelope protein is not ACE2 dependent (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Infection with HIV-1NL pseudotyped with VSV G envelope protein is not ACE2 dependent.
source: Using A549 cells with or without ectopic ACE2 expression, we confirmed that HIV-1NL/SARS-CoV-2 pseudovirus infection is dependent on ACE2, while infection with HIV-1NL pseudotyped instead with VSV G envelope protein is not ACE2 dependent (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Caco2 cells endogenously express ACE2 and TMPRSS2.
source: Caco2 cells, which endogenously express ACE2 and TMPRSS2, show greater susceptibility to SARS-CoV-2 S-pseudotyped HIV-1NL, but equivalent susceptibility to VSV G-pseudotyped HIV-1NL, when compared to A549/ACE2 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Caco2 cells show greater susceptibility to SARS-CoV-2 S-pseudotyped HIV-1NL compared to A549/ACE2 cells.
source: Caco2 cells, which endogenously express ACE2 and TMPRSS2, show greater susceptibility to SARS-CoV-2 S-pseudotyped HIV-1NL, but equivalent susceptibility to VSV G-pseudotyped HIV-1NL, when compared to A549/ACE2 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Caco2 cells show equivalent susceptibility to VSV G-pseudotyped HIV-1NL compared to A549/ACE2 cells.
source: Caco2 cells, which endogenously express ACE2 and TMPRSS2, show greater susceptibility to SARS-CoV-2 S-pseudotyped HIV-1NL, but equivalent susceptibility to VSV G-pseudotyped HIV-1NL, when compared to A549/ACE2 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: TMPRSS2 knockout in Caco2 cells significantly reduced susceptibility to SARS-CoV-2 pseudovirus.
source: To do so, we knocked out TMPRSS2 in ACE2+ TMPRSS2+ Caco2 cells and found that susceptibility to pseudovirus was significantly reduced, comparable to knockout of ACE2 (Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: TMPRSS2 knockout in Caco2 cells reduced susceptibility to pseudovirus comparable to ACE2 knockout.
source: To do so, we knocked out TMPRSS2 in ACE2+ TMPRSS2+ Caco2 cells and found that susceptibility to pseudovirus was significantly reduced, comparable to knockout of ACE2 (Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Camostat and nafamostat reduce pseudovirus entry into control Caco2 cells harboring control sgRNA.
source: Furthermore, both camostat and nafamostat reduce pseudovirus entry into control Caco2 cells harboring control sgRNA, but this trend was lost in cells with two independent TMPRSS2-targeting sgRNAs (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: The effect of camostat and nafamostat on pseudovirus entry was lost in Caco2 cells with TMPRSS2-targeting sgRNAs.
source: Furthermore, both camostat and nafamostat reduce pseudovirus entry into control Caco2 cells harboring control sgRNA, but this trend was lost in cells with two independent TMPRSS2-targeting sgRNAs (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: In the absence of exogenous proteases, TMPRSS2 is a critical host enzyme activating SARS-CoV-2 spike in TMPRSS2+ cells.
source: These data indicate that, in the absence of exogenous proteases, TMPRSS2 is a critical host enzyme activating SARS-CoV-2 spike in TMPRSS2+ cells and that TMPRSS2 is the primary target of camostat and nafamostat in these conditions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the CRISPR knockout and inhibitor data.

claim: TMPRSS2 is the primary target of camostat and nafamostat in TMPRSS2+ cells in the absence of exogenous proteases.
source: These data indicate that, in the absence of exogenous proteases, TMPRSS2 is a critical host enzyme activating SARS-CoV-2 spike in TMPRSS2+ cells and that TMPRSS2 is the primary target of camostat and nafamostat in these conditions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the CRISPR knockout and inhibitor data.

claim: Factor Xa catalyzed S1/S2 cleavage more than an order of magnitude faster than TMPRSS2.
source: Surprisingly, factor Xa catalyzed S1/S2 cleavage more than an order of magnitude faster than TMPRSS2 (Figure 2A–B and D), although factor Xa showed lower affinity (higher Km) compared with TMPRSS2 to the S1/S2 peptide (Figure 2A–B and E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-B and D.

claim: Factor Xa showed lower affinity (higher Km) compared with TMPRSS2 to the S1/S2 peptide.
source: Surprisingly, factor Xa catalyzed S1/S2 cleavage more than an order of magnitude faster than TMPRSS2 (Figure 2A–B and D), although factor Xa showed lower affinity (higher Km) compared with TMPRSS2 to the S1/S2 peptide (Figure 2A–B and E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-B and E.

claim: Thrombin has greater affinity (lower Km) than TMPRSS2 and factor Xa for the S1/S2 substrate.
source: Thrombin has greater affinity (lower Km) than TMPRSS2 and factor Xa for the S1/S2 substrate (Figure 2E) and performs S1/S2 cleavage at a rate intermediate between TMPRSS2 and factor Xa (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D-E.

claim: Thrombin performs S1/S2 cleavage at a rate intermediate between TMPRSS2 and factor Xa.
source: Thrombin has greater affinity (lower Km) than TMPRSS2 and factor Xa for the S1/S2 substrate (Figure 2E) and performs S1/S2 cleavage at a rate intermediate between TMPRSS2 and factor Xa (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Thrombin cleaves the S2' peptide with greater activity than TMPRSS2.
source: Unlike factor Xa, thrombin cleaves the S2' peptide with greater activity than TMPRSS2 (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D-F.

claim: Factor Xa showed ~9-fold greater maximum initial reaction velocity (Vmax) in cleaving the spike S1/S2 peptide compared to cleaving THRBR271 peptide.
source: Remarkably, factor Xa showed ~9-fold greater maximum initial reaction velocity (Vmax) in cleaving the spike S1/S2 peptide compared to cleaving a peptide corresponding to its known substrate, THRBR271 (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The Vmax for thrombin cleavage of the spike S1/S2 peptide was within ~4.5-fold of the Vmax for the FGBR44 peptide.
source: The Vmax for thrombin cleavage of the spike S1/S2 peptide was within ~4.5-fold of the Vmax for the benchmark FGBR44 peptide (Figure 2I), indicating that thrombin might also cleave this site when activated during coagulation.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Thrombin might cleave the S1/S2 site when activated during coagulation.
source: The Vmax for thrombin cleavage of the spike S1/S2 peptide was within ~4.5-fold of the Vmax for the benchmark FGBR44 peptide (Figure 2I), indicating that thrombin might also cleave this site when activated during coagulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the kinetic data.

claim: Substitution of the P1 arginine in the S1/S2 substrate with alanine resulted in a 4-fold reduction in TMPRSS2 cleavage.
source: Substitution of the P1 arginine in the S1/S2 substrate with alanine (S1S2-P1A) resulted in a 4-fold reduction in TMPRSS2 cleavage and abolished nearly all cleavage by factor Xa and thrombin (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: Substitution of the P1 arginine in the S1/S2 substrate with alanine abolished nearly all cleavage by factor Xa and thrombin.
source: Substitution of the P1 arginine in the S1/S2 substrate with alanine (S1S2-P1A) resulted in a 4-fold reduction in TMPRSS2 cleavage and abolished nearly all cleavage by factor Xa and thrombin (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: Substitutions in the P3 and P4 positions (S1S2-HPN) did not change TMPRSS2 cleavage.
source: Substitutions in the P3 and P4 positions (S1S2-HPN) with features typical of a substrate of type II transmembrane serine proteases (TTSPs), a family which includes TMPRSS2 and hepsin (Damalanka et al., 2019), did not change TMPRSS2 cleavage and greatly reduced factor Xa and thrombin cleavage (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: Substitutions in the P3 and P4 positions (S1S2-HPN) greatly reduced factor Xa and thrombin cleavage.
source: Substitutions in the P3 and P4 positions (S1S2-HPN) with features typical of a substrate of type II transmembrane serine proteases (TTSPs), a family which includes TMPRSS2 and hepsin (Damalanka et al., 2019), did not change TMPRSS2 cleavage and greatly reduced factor Xa and thrombin cleavage (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: The cleavage sites of SARS-CoV-2 are specifically cleaved by TMPRSS2, factor Xa, and thrombin.
source: Although the substrate specificity of TTSPs and coagulation factors are not universally similar, the cleavage sites of SARS-CoV-2 are specifically cleaved by TMPRSS2, factor Xa, and thrombin.
evidence: This is an inference based on the substrate specificity data.

claim: The addition of phospholipid vesicles did not change factor Xa activity or substrate preference in the enzymatic assay.
source: The addition of phospholipid vesicles did not change factor Xa activity or substrate preference in this assay (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Addition of purified factor Xa to the media significantly increased rVSV∆G/SARS-CoV-2 pseudovirus infection in Calu3 cells at 16 hr post infection.
source: In the VSV pseudovirus system, addition of purified factor Xa or thrombin to the media significantly increased infection in Calu3 cells 16 hr post infection as determined by either quantification of NeonGreen (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) or nanoluciferase activity (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: The concentration of proteases used in the pseudovirus assay (125-250 nM) are comparable to reference ranges of prothrombin.

claim: Furin was not sensitive to any of the candidate inhibitors.

claim: Coagulation-induced cleavage enhances spike activation and increases viral entry into target cells.
